Modern · The Seoul Table

Baechu Kimchi

A modern, gochujang-enriched kimchi, with bite-size cabbage and a lively ferment.

Korean · Medium · Makes 1 jar (about 1.5 kg)

Jump to recipe ↓

Behind the dish

Lane: modern — the paste-loud build, and the honest confession that comes with it. Straight talk, because this site runs on it: traditional kimchi does not use gochujang. The pot's chile arrives as gochugaru flakes, and any jar telling you otherwise is selling shortcuts. But this site's whole argument is what the paste can do, and in kimchi it does something real — a spoonful in the paste adds the ferment's roundness and a deeper red, a modern build the home fermenters of the last twenty years arrived at honestly. This record makes that jar, labels it plainly, and runs a faster ferment than the traditional batch (kbbqguide#B01's slow 1–3-day room stage) — warmer, shorter, punchier. Heat dial: 3.

The cabbage and salt

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • Brine the cut cabbage in salted water 3 hours (the quick-brine method — squares in a salt solution rather than salted leaf-by-leaf; faster, less traditional, well-suited to the small-cut build). Turn every 45 minutes. Rinse twice, drain 30 minutes, squeeze by the handful.
  • Everything else measured: the paste goes together while the cabbage drains.

Let’s make it.

  1. 01
    The paste whisked into a thick slurry — gochugaru, gochujang, fish sauce, shrimp, garlic, ginger, pear, sugar — then the radish and scallions folded through. Checkpoint — taste on a drained cabbage square: full kimchi register, deeper and rounder than the traditional paste — the gochujang's contribution, arriving as body rather than heat. Slightly too strong is correct; the ferment rounds it.
  2. 02
    The squeezed cabbage and paste massaged together by hand (gloves save your weekend) until every square wears the coat, packed into a clean jar — pressed hard, 3 cm of headspace, weight on top, loose lid. Checkpoint — brine rises over the cabbage within a day; top up with salted water if it lags. Under-liquid is the failure mode, same law as every ferment.
  3. 03
    The faster clock: room temperature 2–4 days at normal kitchen warmth (the traditional batch's window assumes a cooler kitchen), tasting from day two. Checkpoint — the readiness read: lively sourness, steady fizz at a stir, squares still crunchy at the bend. This build's smaller cuts and extra ferment surface run about a day faster than the quartered traditional jar — taste early, refrigerate at the snap-and-sour you want, and eat it through its shorter, punchier arc. Chef’s Note — the confession is the recipe's head, and it bears repeating at the table: this is the modern jar, and the traditional jar (gochugaru-only, slower, quartered) is its own master record at the grill site. The two sit side by side in this corpus deliberately — one for the argument of tradition, one for the argument of the paste — and a fridge with both is a fridge that understands both arguments. Neither jar is wrong; only mislabeling one as the other is.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Brine never coveredUnder-packed or under-saltPress harder; top up with salted water
Squares soft by day threeWarm kitchen, long counter stayRefrigerate at first fizz; taste daily
Paste flavor MIAShy gochujang in a mild jarThe full tablespoon; taste the jar plain first
Fuzzy surface moldAir exposureUnder-brine always; discard fuzzy, keep clean batches

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • Refrigerated, 2–3 weeks on its faster arc — young and crunchy through week one, stew-grade sour by week three. The pasted squares into the jjigae pot (#9) at the elder stage is the arc's whole design.
  • Variations: revert to the traditional paste by dropping the gochujang (the honest A/B test); cucumber squares at a 1-day ferment; the radish-only fork runs the same week's jar.
